Chapter 3: Seeing People—The Shift from Blame to Understanding
There’s this quiet transformation that happens when someone steps out of the box. It’s not about dramatic gestures or big announcements—it usually starts with something simple: you begin to actually see others as people, not just as objects or obstacles in your way.
Think about a team leader who’s frustrated because a colleague keeps missing deadlines. For weeks, the leader’s been venting to others, stuck replaying every missed deadline over and over, and honestly, just avoiding a real, honest conversation. Then, one day after a tense meeting, the leader pauses. Instead of falling back on those old complaints, they start to wonder: what’s really going on with that colleague? Is there something happening in their life that no one knows about? Maybe they’re struggling. Maybe it’s not about slacking off at all.
That tiny flash of curiosity changes everything.
When you start seeing other people as individuals—with their own hopes, fears, and challenges—it gets harder to blame and so much easier to connect. The leader, now open to understanding, finally reaches out. And the conversation? It’s different this time. It’s not about pointing fingers. It’s about support. The colleague, feeling that shift, opens up about a family crisis weighing them down. Suddenly, solutions show up—not because the problem magically vanished, but because the relationship changed.
This is what getting “out of the box” really means. It’s not about ignoring real issues or pretending everything’s fine. It’s about recognizing that everyone’s just as real, just as complicated, and just as human as you are. When you see that, blame fades and understanding takes its place. Defensiveness melts into true cooperation.
You’ve probably had moments like this, even if just for a second. Maybe you’re a parent, and after a shouting match with your teenager, you suddenly remember what it was like to be that age. Or maybe you’re a manager, and after a tough talk, you realize your team member’s resistance is rooted in fear, not laziness. In those moments, the walls of the box start to crumble.
The truth is, getting out of the box isn’t a one-time thing. It’s a practice—a way of showing up for every interaction with openness and humility. It’s being willing to question your own assumptions, to listen more than you talk, and to look for the real person behind someone’s behavior.
What’s really powerful is the ripple effect. When one person steps out of the box, others often follow. A leader who listens builds trust. A friend who apologizes opens the door for honesty. Over time, relationships shift—they become less about winning or losing, and more about working together.
Of course, staying out of the box isn’t always easy. Old habits kick in, especially when stress hits. It’s so tempting to justify yourself, to blame, or just to pull away. The key is to notice when it’s happening, pause for a moment, and choose again. Every moment gives you a fresh chance to see others with new eyes.
